subject: Closing 1000 W Crossing
comment: Somehow it had escaped my attention that it was on the table to close the 1000 W crossing until I read articles about it today. To abandon access and deprive an isolated neighborhood of one of its few connections is not an acceptable solution to the quiet zone problem in my opinion. And for up to two years? It is crazy to me, honestly, I can't see how councilmembers Petro and Puy in particular might find "relief" in closing one of only four streets that connect Fairpark and Poplar Grove. This is a failure, not a solution, and will no doubt exacerbate issues the nearby community has fought hard to minimize, this smacks of the same sort of thinking that led to the closure of the adjacent Madsen Park and the Jordan River trail a block and a half away. If there's a problem on the west side, it's cheaper and easier to just remove the minority than fix the problem.... It's a troubling pattern, one that has impacted this particular area way to much lately.

subject: Why a "troika" for leadership is worrisome
comment: Chris-Thank you for attending the Greater Avenues meeting last Wednesday and mentioning that the City Council is considering a reorganization of leadership for positions on the Council and the RDA. The Council can certainly change its own organization under Policy and Procedures. I don't know enough about the RDA's governance to know whether the Council has the authority to make that change unilaterally without a public process. As I said at the Avenues meeting, I consider the proposal worrisome for the following reasons: -the inefficiency of having such a major leadership position turn over every year -the potential for competition with the Mayor's office and -the inequity of making the position of chair so time-consuming that some members of the Council could not assume it because of other responsibilities. Since my remarks last week, I've also thought about the possible changes in membership on the Council coming up in a year. Based on what I am hearing, 2 members of the Council have said that they will not run for re-election. That means that we start 2026 with AT MOST 5 experienced members of the Council, possibly fewer, maybe 3. Back to the issue of equity: Under the proposal, one of these experienced Council members would have to step up to the lead position. It is not a matter of 1 out of 7 having the time to do it; the horizon is that 1 out of 5 would need to be ready. And it couldn't be the same as the Council member who served in 2025. The proposal requires that in the year 2026, one out of at most 4 Council members has to be ready to step into what I view as a full-time job. That's how I see the proposal over the next 15 months.....too few people available. In short, I do not think that now is the time for an experiment with the organization of leadership. Respectfully, Cindy C. -

subject: Title 18 Feedback
comment: SLC Community Council Title 18 Contributors RE: Title 18 Feedback Dear SLC Community Council Members and Title 18 contributors, Thank you for your ongoing efforts on Title 18. Based on listening to your sessions on this topic, and my own experience on how vacant properties have negatively impacted my own neighborhood, my thoughts and recommendations for some meaningful measures to make owners of vacant properties properly maintain them are as follows: 1) Small claims court thresholds are so low, many developers see these low fees/fines as preferable to the cost of maintaining secure, safe, clean buildings & landscapes. 2) Penalties for non-compliance should be relative to the property value and offer a pain threshold high enough so that it is a clear financial benefit to comply. 3) Extension Requests on property approvals, not "permitted" within the 1-year approval period, and not maintained within SLC guidelines, should be declined. 4) Severe penalties, against owners of neglected properties, must be made when vacant properties become the burden of the Police and Fire Departments. 5) A tally should be kept of non-compliant properties, resulting in a rating scale for owner property maintenance compliance. This rating should be considered during the approval process for design reviews, planning reviews and permit approvals. Safe, vibrant and secure communities are the result of people investing in those communities, living there, making them better and maintaining them. When properties are left vacant and neglected by owners, it shows a lack of care or investment in the community, and invites vandalism, crime and fire risks. Please make Title 18th strong enough to stop these multi-year blights, and crime magnates perpetuating within our communities. Sincerely, Anne Ruth Isaacson

subject: Comment for the Council
comment: Honorable Salt Lake City Council, I am writing to you all today to make sure my voice is heard on a few very important things that our city, county, and state can be working on. You all know who I am, but what you might not know about me is that I am an environmentalist, author, cyclist, and urbanist. My current passion is the Rio Grande Plan, a citizen-led proposal to bury the rails beginning at 1300 South and re-emerging at 600 North, rerouting the tracks to the historic rail corridor along 500 West and utilizing the iconic Rio Grande Depot as Utah's Central Station. While yes, I know that there are differing opinions on where to bury the tracks—or even if burying the tracks is the best way to ease the socioeconomic divide of East and West Salt Lake County residents—or how to minimize stalled cars polluting our air at ever longer train stops, or if utilizing the historic Rio Grande Depot as Utah's Central Station would enhance the FrontRunner and Trax experience and thus increase ridership. Those points can be debated for years as they have been since 1999 when the choice was made to build Salt Lake Central Station. It's my opinion we cannot keep studying the same thing repeatedly—we must move forward with the Rio Grande Plan. This leads to my second concern: the Green Loop. The Green Loop is a beautiful concept that will transform downtown SLC, but it will die on the vine if it is not properly deployed and properly funded. The way to get at least part of the Green Loop completed is to fund it completely or partially under the Rio Grande Plan. The 500 West street will need to be reconstructed after the Rio Grande Plan train box is installed. That gives the opportunity to aid in the Mayor's plan without disrupting the Rio Grande Plan and it allows for the cost of the Green Loop (along 500 West—at a minimum) to be covered by federal and state funds. This all leads to the completion of a major goal of SLC RDA: revitalization and expansion of the Granary and Depot Districts. It's not just the central downtown area that will see significant changes. The Hardware District and Guadalupe Neighborhood will get a better East to West connection downtown. The Depot District will continue to falter if the principal barrier remains—the railroad tracks. We must have a holistic plan that brings all these visions together. We as residents owe it to ourselves and our community members to get this right. We will have the eyes of the world on us during the 2034 Winter Olympics, and what an amazing statement if we can showcase the Rio Grande Depot. A historic building at the center of it all with a revitalized Depot District, a connection to all forms of transit including Frontrunner, state sponsored Amtrak service, Trax, Buses, and walking and biking via the Green Loop. Imagine an Olympic staging area in front of the Rio Grande Depot along the new Green Loop....This CAN happen but only if you, the council, will this into existence. Let's get a holistic plan for the west side of Salt Lake City's downtown. Let's make the Depot District GRANDE again, starting with the Rio Grande Plan, the Green Loop, and the re-imagined Depot District. Let's honor the state's past by preparing for the future. One day in the not-to-distant future, you, me, our kids and grandkids will take an escalator up from the arriving train platform, enter the beautiful, historic depot to experience a moment of our state's shared past before stepping out into its ever-changing future. We can do this. We've done big things like this before. We can do it again. This is a land of dreamers and the home of the brave, this is Salt Lake City, Utah. I'm here and more than willing to help in any way I can to make the Rio Grande Plan part of Salt Lake's and Utah's future. I hope you will join me. Respectfully, Frederick Jenny
